title: Excavations at Kiriath-jearim near Jerusalem, 2017: Preliminary Report
author: Israel Finkelstein; Thomas Römer; Christophe Nicolle; Zachary C. Dunseth; Assaf Kleiman; et al.
allowedUseNotes: Copyrighted peer-reviewed excavation report. Project stores its own summary of the site's identification and excavation results only; no reproduction of the report's text, plans, or photographs.
summary: Preliminary report on the first (2017) season of the Shmunis Family Excavations at Kiriath-jearim, a joint Tel Aviv University/Collège de France project directed by Israel Finkelstein and Thomas Römer, the first significant excavation at the site. The report treats the identification of the site with Deir el-Azhar (also transliterated Deir el-'Azar), the hill above modern Abu Ghosh, as effectively settled in the field -- first proposed by L.-H. Vincent in 1907 on the strength of two preserved place-names ("Deir el-Azar" preserving the name of Eleazar, who in 1 Samuel 7:1 is consecrated to guard the ark at Kiriath-jearim, and "Qaryat al-'Inab," the town's former Arabic name, preserving "Kiriath") and reinforced by the site's fit with the narrative's own geography, on the historical route between the coastal plain and Jerusalem. The excavation itself found the tell to be one of the largest Iron Age mounds in the central highlands (a summit area on the order of 250 x 250 m), and its headline discovery was a massive rectangular platform at the summit, built of large worked stones, which the excavators date to around the first half of the 8th century BCE and tentatively associate with a Northern Kingdom construction project (comparable in scale to other large Iron Age platforms/podia elsewhere in the region) rather than with any structure from David's own, earlier period; the same platform was reused and reinforced in the Iron IIC and Hellenistic periods (the latter phase tentatively linked to the Seleucid general Bacchides' fortification campaign named in 1 Maccabees 9:50-52), with a further Roman-period military-camp phase on top. This project cites the report for the site's identification, which the field treats as secure, and for confirming that this is a genuine, substantial Iron Age highland tell -- not for any claim about the site's much earlier (Iron I, eleventh/tenth-century BCE) form during the period this project's own perez-uzzah scene depicts, which these preliminary results do not describe in comparable detail (see confidenceNotes).

A full excavation monograph, Kiriath-jearim: The Shmunis Family Excavations (Finkelstein and Römer, eds., Emery and Claire Yass Publications in Archaeology / Monograph Series of the Sonia and Marco Nadler Institute of Archaeology no. 45, Eisenbrauns/Penn State University Press, 2025), has since been published and would supersede this preliminary report as the fuller primary reference; it has not been consulted for this card and is flagged here as a natural next step rather than adopted sight-unseen.
